title: Armed Forces Pension Scheme 2015 (CAS-105605-Z1T5)
text:
CAS-105605-Z1T5
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mrs E
Scheme Armed Forces Pension Scheme 2015 (AFPS 15)
Respondent Veterans UK
Outcome
Complaint summary
Mrs E has complained that she has not been awarded the appropriate tier of ill health
early retirement (IHER) benefits by Veterans UK. She contends that her level of
benefit should be upgraded to Tier 2 in the AFPS 15.
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The AFPS 151 was introduced on 1 April 2015 under the Public Service Pensions Act
2013 (the Act). The relevant provisions are contained in The Armed Forces Pension
Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2336) (as amended) (the 2014 Regulations) and The
Armed Forces Early Departure Payments Scheme Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2328)
(EDPS 2014).
The Normal Pension Age (NPA) and Deferred Pension Age (DPA) for the AFPS 15
are determined in accordance with section 10 of the Act.
In general, both the NPA and DPA for a member must be:
• the same as the member’s State Pension Age (SPA); or
• 65 if that is higher
However, for members of the armed forces2, the NPA is 60.
1 The AFPS 15 is a career average revalued earnings (CARE) scheme.
2 This means the naval, military and air forces of the Crown.
1

CAS-105605-Z1T5
Three tiers of benefit are available for members of the AFPS 15 who leave the armed
forces as a result of ill health. The level of benefit is related to the severity of the
impact the individual’s condition has on their capacity for civilian employment. Tier 1
is awarded to those who were unable to do their service job, but whose ability to
undertake other gainful employment is not considered to be significantly impaired.
Tier 2 is awarded to those whose ability to undertake other gainful employment is
significantly impaired. Tier 3 is awarded to those who are permanently incapable of
any full-time employment.
Relevant extracts from the aforementioned provisions are provided in Appendix One.
Mrs E is a member of the AFPS 15.
Mrs E was medically discharged from the armed forces in February 2022. She was
then age 46. The Medical Board Record3 (F Med 23) noted her principal conditions
as: (a) knee pain and tremor; and (b) carpal and cubital tunnel syndrome with upper
limb tremor and weakness. Mrs E was also diagnosed with “adjustment disorder” and
back pain4.
Decisions on applications for IHER are made by Veterans UK under delegated
authority from the Secretary of State, “the scheme manager”.
In its letter dated 22 February 2022, Veterans UK informed Mrs E that she had been
awarded5 Tier 1 benefits from the AFPS 15, that is, a deferred pension for payment at
her SPA6 and a Tier 1 lump sum of £30,177.66 payable immediately on discharge.
Mrs E requested a review of her Tier 1 award by Veterans UK under the AFPS 15
Internal Dispute Resolution Procedure (IDRP) for the following reasons:-
• She believed that it should have awarded her Tier 2 benefits from the AFPS 15.
• She had not been able to work since leaving service and did not envisage “a
return to work any time soon”.
• The “complexity” of her mental and physical health issues meant she was
incapable of holding down regular employment.
3 The Medical Board met on 10 August 2021 and agreed that Mrs E was permanently unfit for military service
and should be recommended for medical discharge. It also requested that Mrs E’s contract be extended by
six months to enable “further investigation, treatment and rehabilitation”.
4 Mrs E’s adjustment disorder and back pain did not lead to her discharge.
5 Veterans UK agreed with the medical advice given by its Medical Advisor in December 2021 that Mrs E
satisfied the conditions for Tier 1 benefits from the AFPS 15. Further details may be found in paragraphs 16
and 19.
6 Mrs E’s SPA is currently 67.
2

CAS-105605-Z1T5
• Her current medication did not effectively treat her conditions.
• She received Personal Independence Payments (PIP) from the Department for
Work and Pensions.
Mrs E provided additional medical evidence from her: (a) Consultant Orthopaedic
Surgeon; (b) Consultant Neurologist; and (c) Neurology Clinic in support of her
appeal.
In October 2022, Veterans UK sought the assistance of its Medical Advisor (MA) in
order to carry out the review.
The MA informed Veterans UK that:-
• It had originally considered Mrs E’s case in December 2021. It advised at the time
that she was unfit for employment but there were several issues which meant that
her long-term prognosis was unclear. So it recommended that Mrs E should
receive Tier 1 benefits from the AFPS 15.
• Mrs E had now provided new medical information. However, it was “no further
forward in terms of forming an opinion on her long-term prognosis”.
The MA consequently asked Veterans UK to seek further medical evidence from Mrs
E’s treating doctors before providing its advice.
In January 2023, Veterans UK received this further evidence and gave it to the MA.
The MA reviewed the available medical documents and said that:
“[Mrs E] originally injured her left knee in October 2018 following a fall from a
top bunk. She recovered from this following physiotherapy. She injured her left
knee again in October 2019 when she slipped on a ladder and twisted her
knee. She was diagnosed with an avulsion fracture and possible MCL rupture
and was noted to have severe degenerative changes in the patellofemoral
compartment. She also developed involuntary movements of the left foot.
There was conflicting opinion on management but surgery appears to have
been ruled out at this time and she was admitted for a 2 week rehab
programme…
She was also troubled by bilateral upper and lower limb tremors and
weakness of her grip. Tremor had been present in her left leg since the
second injury to her knee in October 2019. The cause of neurological
symptoms was unknown.
Regarding her function at the time of the board, she had full range of
movement of her left lower limb but it was constantly painful. She could walk
but with pain. She could manage stairs but would avoid when possible. She
could walk her dog but only ‘around the block’. Sleep was poor. Driving
caused pain. She had difficulty gripping to chop veg and use a tin opener.
3

CAS-105605-Z1T5
[Mrs E] was also diagnosed with an adjustment disorder in service which was
felt to be related to her physical health conditions and discharge from service.
She was under the care of a CPN at DCMH but does not appear to have been
seen by a Consultant. She was prescribed medication and low intensity
psychological therapy. At the time of the original tier advice she was still under
specialist review, waiting on appointments with orthopaedics and neurology. A
Tier 1 was advised given her age, diagnostic uncertainty and possible
improvement with further treatment.
Since the original tier review updated medical evidence has been provided.
[Mrs E] has been followed-up by a neurology Consultant in March and
November last year. In his letter of March 2022 the Consultant notes ongoing
‘occasional severe jerks that can wake her up in the night’ and ‘only the left leg
is involved’. He also notes that she had experienced pain from the elbow to
the fingers in the left arm followed by the right arm and this was attributed to
use of crutches. There was no suggestion this was an ongoing problem with
the upper limbs. There was no muscle wasting noted in the limbs but
occasional jerking of the foot was observed and she walked with a limp. She
was commenced on a medication to try and help with the involuntary
movements of the foot. Nerve conduction studies of the upper and lower limbs
were repeated in April 2022 and found to be normal. MRI scans of the brain
and spine have identified some degenerative change in the spine only. At
follow-up in November 2022 there had been some improvement with
medication but her memory had been affected. A functional neurological
disorder (FND) was considered and [Mrs E] was referred to neuropsychology.
In his letter of referral Dr Steiger notes that trauma can be associated with
dystonia. He was concerned that trauma could be impacting on her ability to
recover. He also notes ongoing pension issues and a tribunal case relating to
a claim regarding her injuries. The outcome of her referral to neuropsychology
is not yet known.
She has also been reviewed by orthopaedics in September 2022. At this point
she presented with pain in multiple joints, including her left knee, right knee,
ankles, hips and lower back. Her walking distance was a few hundred yards
but could be less when symptoms are at their worst. She had started using a
walking stick. It was felt that her symptoms could not all be explained by the
degenerative changes in her knee. She was to have further investigation for
inflammatory joint disease and it was also noted that polyarthralgia is common
in menopausal women. It was suggested that HRT7 could be an option to help
her joint pains and she was keen to try a course of this.
The future course of her health still remains unknown but improvement is
possible. The diagnosis remains unclear, with no clear physical cause for her
neurological symptoms identified. A FND has been suggested as a cause but
7 HRT is an acronym for Hormone Replacement Therapy.
4

CAS-105605-Z1T5
this has not yet been confirmed. If following further assessment FND is
diagnosed then there is still the possibility that her condition may improve. This
would involve an MDT approach involving psychotherapists, physiotherapists
and OTs. As pointed out by Dr Steiger the impact of trauma had not yet been
addressed. It is also possible that ongoing pension and tribunal issues may be
impacting on her symptoms.
There is the possibility that her joint pains may improve with HRT. If any
inflammatory joint disease is identified then this could be improved with
appropriate specialist medication…
The main issue is her joint pain, particularly in the left knee and involuntary
movement of the left leg. This affects her ability to walk and she is limited to a
few hundred yards. There was no suggestion in the recent letters that she has
any significant functional impairment of the upper limbs. From a physical
perspective she should be capable of a sedentary desk-based role. I note that
her memory had been affected by medication but it is unclear to what degree
this impacted her function. Should it affect her ability to function I would expect
that it would be withdrawn. The notes prior to discharge state that she was
setting up a small business selling candles online. Having reviewed the
updated evidence I remain of the opinion that it does not support that she will
be significantly limited in her ability to achieve gainful civilian employment until
retirement age. Her mobility appears to be the main limiting factor and she
should be capable of a sedentary role. There is also the possibility that her
condition can improve with further input and time.
A Tier 1 is advised.”
• Her appeal had been considered by the Deciding Officer (DO).
• The DO, after carefully reviewing all the available evidence, decided that the rules
of the AFPS 15 had been applied8.
• So her appeal had been rejected.
Relevant paragraphs from the IDRP decision letter dated 7 March 2023 to Mrs E
including the opinions expressed by the MA are set out in Appendix Two.
Following the complaint being referred to The Pensions Ombudsman, Mrs E and
Veterans UK made further submissions that have been summarised in paragraph 23
to 28 below.
8 Relevant paragraphs from the DO’s decision dated 6 March 2023 are set out in Appendix Two.
5

CAS-105605-Z1T5
“They medically discharged me as they said I was not capable of fulfilling my
role as a soldier and a chef. I asked if I could stay as a pay clerk, my other
trade and they said no. I did not want to leave…a career I loved for 29 years.
So if they did not wish to continue to employ me why would anyone else want
to employ me?”
She has now been diagnosed as also suffering from fibromyalgia caused by “trauma”
to her body.
Her local council has: (a) awarded her a disablement grant; and (b) provided her with
a wet room and a stair lift in her home.
Veterans UK’s position
It should like to sincerely apologise to Mrs E for sending the IDRP decision letter to
her old home address by mistake.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
6

CAS-105605-Z1T5
It was not disputed that Mrs E was permanently unfit for military service and that she
was currently unable to work. What was disputed was whether Mrs E’s capacity for
gainful employment was significantly impaired to her NPA of 60.
Members’ entitlements to benefits when taking early retirement due to ill health were
determined by the relevant scheme rules or regulations. The scheme rules or
regulations determined the circumstances in which members were eligible for ill
health benefits, the conditions which they must satisfy, and the way in which
decisions about ill health benefits must be taken.
In this case, the relevant rules for the AFPS 15 are regulations 51 (Tier 3), 52 (Tier 2)
and 58 of the 2014 Regulations and regulation 19 (Tier 1) of EDPS 2014.
Under regulation 58 because Mrs E was awarded Tier 1 on service discharge, the
review was limited to considering whether she satisfied the conditions for Tier 2
benefits set out in regulation 52.
A Tier 2 pension would be paid under regulation 52 if, in the opinion of the scheme
manager, (a) Mrs E had suffered a breakdown in health, as a result of which, her
capacity for any gainful employment was significantly impaired; and (b) the
breakdown would continue until Mrs E reached NPA.
The term “significantly impaired” is not defined in the 2014 Regulations. However,
regulation 51 required that if an applicant was permanently incapable of full-time
employment, he/she qualified for the higher benefit in regulation 54. So it followed
that the lower benefit in regulation 55 was payable where there was a lesser degree
of incapacity and this must mean the applicant was capable of some form of full-time
employment.
Consequently, if Mrs E did not qualify for a Tier 2 pension it must be because
Veterans UK took the view that she was, or would be before NPA, capable of
undertaking some form of full-time employment. That employment did not have to be
the same or similar to the role she undertook in the armed forces, but it must be full-
time.
The decision as to whether Mrs E satisfied the conditions for Tier 2 benefits was for
Veterans UK on behalf of the scheme manager, the Secretary of State, to make.
Before making its decision, regulation 58 required Veterans UK to have consulted
with the MA as to Mrs E’s capacity for any full-time employment. Veterans UK was
not, however, bound by any advice it received from its MA. It was still expected to
reach a decision of its own. That being said, the weight which Veterans UK placed on
any evidence relating to Mrs E’s case was for it to decide. It was open to Veterans UK
to accept the advice of its MA; unless there was good reason for it not to do so. The
kind of things the Adjudicator had in mind were errors or omissions of fact or a
misunderstanding of the relevant rules by the MA.
7

CAS-105605-Z1T5
MAs do not come within the PO’s jurisdiction as far as their medical opinions are
concerned. They are answerable to their own professional bodies and the General
Medical Council. The PO would simply consider whether the MAs provided sufficient
and appropriate advice which it was reasonable for Veterans UK to rely on when
making its decision. It was accepted that Veterans UK could only review medical
advice from a lay perspective and could not be expected to challenge a medical
opinion as such.
The decision to award Mrs E Tier 1 benefits was made by Veterans UK in February
2022. Veterans UK accepted the medical view of its MA that, based on the available
evidence at the time, Mrs E was unfit for employment but she only satisfied the
conditions for payment of Tier 1 benefits as her long-term prognosis was unclear.
Mrs E was dissatisfied with the outcome of her IHER application and appealed it
under the IDRP. After carrying out a thorough assessment, the DO concluded that
her appeal should be rejected because:-
• It was satisfied that the original tier decision was correct and that Tier 1 benefits
were appropriate.
• It concurred with the opinions of the MA and Mrs E’s treating doctors that her
symptoms were potentially functional rather than physical. Further psychological
input was consequently necessary in order to fully understand her conditions and
treat them effectively in the long term.
• The medical evidence available did not show that Mrs E was significantly impaired
from achieving full-time employment until NPA.
• It agreed with the MA that Mrs E should be capable of a sedentary role.
• As Mrs E’s prognosis was unclear until further medical investigations into the
cause for her neurological symptoms had been completed, it could not say that
Mrs E was, more likely than not, unable to achieve employment and remain so
until age 60.
• When these investigations were complete, Veterans UK could consider her case
further.
Mrs E has asserted that Veterans UK did not take into account all of the medical
evidence when reaching its decision during the IDRP.
However, in its decision dated 6 March 2023, the DO said that it had reviewed all the
available medical evidence including: (a) F Med 23; (b) the MA’s medical opinion; and
(c) a substantial amount of civilian medical evidence dealing with Mrs E’s physical
and mental health conditions. The DO also said that Veterans UK had obtained
8

CAS-105605-Z1T5
further medical evidence9 and this was also considered to gain a full picture of her
current level of function, limitations, and likely progression of her conditions.
So, the Adjudicator was satisfied that Veterans UK had considered all the medical
evidence that pertained to Mrs E’s conditions at the relevant time when making its
decision.
Mrs E had also said Veterans UK ignored that: (a) she was injured while serving on a
Royal Navy warship; and (b) she was not informed of the appropriate health and
safety procedures. In the Adjudicator’s view, these were irrelevant factors in the
assessment of her eligibility for IHER benefits from the AFPS 15 and Veterans UK
could consequently disregard them.
The Adjudicator had not identified any obvious error or omission of fact, irrelevant
matters or misunderstanding of the relevant regulations in the MA’s advice which
Veterans UK should have queried.
So, it was the Adjudicator’s view that there was no reason why Veterans UK should
not have accepted the advice it received from its MA in reaching its decision in Mrs
E’s case.
The fact that Mrs E was still suffering from the same medical conditions did not, in
and of itself, invalidate Veterans UK’s decision. Veterans UK could only be expected
to make its decision based on the medical opinions expressed at the time pertaining
to her health when her employment ended. Veterans UK chose to prefer the opinion
of its MAs, who were experts in occupational health.
It was consequently the Adjudicator’s opinion that Veterans UK took appropriate
action during the IDRP after obtaining a further medical opinion from its MA. He was
also satisfied that Veterans UK: (a) gave proper consideration to Mrs E’s application
at the time by assessing all the relevant medical evidence available, and (b) acted in
accordance with the relevant regulations and the principles outlined in paragraph 31
above.
Mrs E had said that she was in receipt of PIP from the DWP. Receipt of these
benefits did not, however, mean that Mrs E would automatically qualify for Tier 2
9 This included: (a) Mrs E’s service medical records; (b) consultancy neurology letters; and (c) letters from
her Community Mental Health Nurse.
9

CAS-105605-Z1T5
benefits from the AFPS 15 because the criteria used to determine whether or not she
qualified for PIP are different and less stringent.
Mrs E did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion and the complaint was passed to me
to consider. Mrs E and Veterans UK provided their further comments which do not
change the outcome.
Mrs E’s further comments
She was medically discharged from the armed forces in February 2022 before: (a) the
completion of specialist investigations into her medical condition10; (b) the
confirmation of diagnosis; (c) the establishment of prognosis; and (d) a full
understanding of the long-term impact of her conditions.
In August 2021, the Medical Board requested that her contract be extended by six
months to enable further investigation, treatment and rehabilitation. So her medical
condition had not been “fully diagnosed, stabilised, or properly assessed at the time
discharge action proceeded.”
Prior to her medical discharge, she was denied access to the full level of specialist
military medical care, investigation, and assessment that she should reasonably have
expected under “military medical policy and duty of care obligations”.
If she had been referred to military neurology specialists whilst in service, “diagnosis,
prognosis, permanence, and functional impact could have been established
significantly sooner and before final discharge and pension determinations were
made.”
Instead, because medical discharge was already being pursued, she was effectively
left to await NHS investigations after discharge.
This created a fundamentally unfair position whereby discharge and pension and
decisions were being made without the full medical evidence being available.
While the Army could, in practice, under “Queen’s Regulations” begin or complete the
discharge process whilst she remained under medical investigation, the critical issue
was whether her “medical condition had been sufficiently stabilised and fully
assessed to allow a lawful and fair decision regarding discharge, employability,
pension entitlement, and compensation.”
The “PAP10 PULHHEEMS Administrative Pamphlet” governs Army medical grading
and states that discharge action should be based upon proper medical assessment of
employability and fitness for service. In particular, it states:
10 Mrs E was still awaiting neurology and orthopaedic referrals for “formal diagnosis and specialist
assessment”.
10

CAS-105605-Z1T5
“Only if other employment is not possible and if transfer to another corps is not
authorised should a soldier be discharged.”
“AGAI Volume 2 Chapter 78 Table 6” provides guidance regarding the management
of medically downgraded personnel and says that personnel may be considered non-
deployable where they are:
“Unable to perform primary employment / CEG with reasonable adaptation
and restrictions” and “Unable to work effectively for 32.5 hours per week.”
She says that:
“Without confirmed diagnosis and specialist evidence, I do not believe the
Army could reasonably determine:
• whether my condition was temporary or permanent,
• whether my condition would significantly impair future employment,
• whether my condition was attributable or aggravated by service,
• whether I met the AGAI Vol 2 Ch 78 Table 6 criteria regarding
employability and working capacity,
• or what level of pension and compensation entitlement I should receive.
I respectfully submit that this raises serious questions regarding:
• whether my future civilian employability was properly assessed,
• whether the severity and permanence of my condition were fully
understood,
• whether the correct AFPS ill-health tier was awarded,
• and whether the Medical Board conclusions were internally consistent
with the pension determination reached.
…the available evidence suggests that the impact of my medical condition
upon long-term civilian employability may have been significantly
underestimated because specialist investigations and diagnosis remained
incomplete at the time discharge and pension decisions were made.
I further believe that proceeding with discharge before completion of specialist
investigations was contrary to:
• the principles of procedural fairness,
• proper medical assessment requirements,
• AGAI Vol 2 Ch 78 Table 6 guidance,
11

CAS-105605-Z1T5
• PAP10 procedures,
• and the Army’s duty of care obligations owed to serving personnel
undergoing medical discharge.
I therefore maintain that:
• my discharge process was premature,
• my medical grading may have been inaccurate,
• my prognosis was not fully established,
• my long-term employability had not been properly assessed,
• and my pension and compensation entitlement may have been
materially prejudiced by decisions being made without complete
medical evidence…
I further request consideration of:
• whether my condition had been deemed sufficiently “stable” for pension
purposes,
• whether ongoing investigations were properly considered by the
Medical Board,
• whether deferral of discharge pending specialist investigations was
considered,
• whether the Army acted fairly in refusing specialist military referral due
to impending discharge,
• whether AGAI Vol 2 Ch 78 Table 6 procedures were properly followed,
• whether I was denied appropriate access to military specialist
investigation and treatment pathways,
• and whether my AFPS and AFCS11 assessments should now be
reconsidered in light of subsequent medical evidence and diagnosis.”
Following her medical discharge, she was informed by the consultants treating her
that her condition was linked to the trauma she sustained during her accident at work.
She now also suffers from fibromyalgia which significantly affects her daily functioning
and ability to work. This diagnosis demonstrates that her condition was more serious
than originally assessed at the time of her discharge.
11 AFCS is an acronym for the Armed Forces Compensation Scheme.
12

CAS-105605-Z1T5
She has now been informed that she cannot have HRT and this restricts her ability to
manage her condition effectively.
At the time of her discharge, she was informed that she was deemed unemployable
either as a chef or a pay clerk, her two trained roles. So she had been assessed as
being unfit to continue in both a physically demanding role and a sedentary role. She
consequently finds it difficult to understand how the conclusion that she could be
employable in a civilian environment was reached.
Prior to her discharge, she had to submit formal service complaints in order to ensure
that her two accidents at work were properly recorded.
In June 2021, her complaint to the Service Complaints Ombudsman for the Armed
Forces was upheld. As a result, her accident report was amended to accurately
reflect her circumstances12. She is consequently concerned that the information
which Veterans UK relied upon to assess her IHER application may not be complete
or accurate.
She was not given reasonable opportunity to: (a) provide updated evidence; (b)
discuss her application before a decision was made; or (c) present her case during
the original appeal process.
She says that:
“Since my discharge, I have not been able to return to employment. My
conditions affect my reliability, mobility, and ability to function consistently on a
day-to-day basis. In addition, my PTSD and adjustment disorder impact my
mental resilience, concentration, and ability to cope with workplace pressures.
For example, on days when my symptoms are severe, I may struggle to get
moving in the morning, which would make it difficult to attend work regularly or
meet the expectations of an employer.
I was advised by the Ministry of Defence that I was not considered employable
in either of my dual trades. In my view, the limitations I experience would also
significantly restrict my ability to undertake alternative forms of employment,
particularly those requiring consistent attendance, mobility, sustained physical
effort, or mental resilience.
12 Mrs E informed the Service Complaints Ombudsman for the Armed Forces that the original accident
report was incorrect in the following ways:
“ a. The washing up liquid had not spread slightly, it was a more significant spread;
b. I was ordered to clean the locker. I did not take it upon myself. I was not told to wait until later in the
week;
c. I was able to explain what happened when the First Aiders arrived at the scene;
d. The bags I was carrying up the ladder were light, not heavy;
e. I was MFD and cleared to return to the ship following a previous injury from which I had recovered;
f. I was not off the ship for 20 months following the previous injury, it was 8 months”.
13

CAS-105605-Z1T5
I have been working with Universal Credit support services to try to establish a
business that would allow me to work in a way that accommodates my
disabilities. However, this is still in its early stages and is not currently
generating an income. This reflects my need to attempt flexible and highly
adapted work, rather than being able to engage in standard employment.”
Veterans UK’s further comments
Mrs E is eligible to request a review of her tier classification within five years of the
date of her medical discharge in February 2022 if she believes there has been a
deterioration in her medical condition since then.
I note the additional points raised by Mrs E but I agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
• the appropriate evidence had been obtained and considered;
• the applicable scheme rules and regulations have been correctly applied; and
• the decision was supported by the available relevant evidence.
Veterans UK was required to assess Mrs E’s IHER application in accordance with the
2014 Regulations, and to do so in consultation with its MA.
Mrs E contends that Veterans UK’s decision to award her Tier 1 benefits from the
AFPS 15 was improperly made without full medical evidence available because, at
the time of her medical discharge in February 2022, her medical condition had not yet
been fully diagnosed, stabilised, and properly assessed.
So, in her view, Veterans UK had significantly underestimated the impact of her
medical condition upon her long-term civilian employability when reaching its decision
14

CAS-105605-Z1T5
without confirmation of diagnosis, establishment of prognosis and a full understanding
of her condition.
Mrs E has also alleged that she was unfairly discharged from the armed forces
prematurely before her medical condition had been fully diagnosed, stabilised, and
properly assessed, She has provided a detailed explanation as to why she believes
this to be the case as summarised in her further comments above.
Mrs E’s complaint that the process used to medically discharge her from the armed
forces is, however, a matter of employment law. This is also the case for many of her
other serious allegations including that she was denied access to appropriate
specialist military medical care, investigation, and assessment prior to her discharge.
It is not within my jurisdiction to investigate such allegations. These are dealt with
primarily by the courts or employment tribunals. I shall consequently not consider
them further here.
There is no dispute that, at the time Veterans UK decided to award Mrs E Tier 1
benefits from the AFPS 15 in February 2022, the long term prognosis of her condition
was unclear.
When Veterans UK sought the assistance of its MA in October 2022 to carry out a
review of its decision as requested by Mrs E, the MA acknowledged this and said
that, at the time it originally considered Mrs E’s IHER application in December 2021,
she was still under specialist review with outstanding appointments with orthopaedics
and neurology. So, the MA had recommended that Mrs E should receive Tier 1
benefits from the AFPS 15 given her age, diagnostic uncertainty and possible
improvement with further treatment.
However, despite having received additional medical evidence from Mrs E in support
of her appeal under the IDRP, the MA was still unable to form a medical view on Mrs
E’s long-term prognosis. It consequently asked Veterans UK to seek further medical
evidence from Mrs E’s treating doctors before providing its advice.
This was obtained and then passed to the MA. It is clear from the advice which the
MA gave Veterans UK that it had taken some time to review Mrs E’s case and its
advice was based on a careful examination of all the then available relevant evidence
including the medical reports prepared following her appointments with orthopaedics
and neurology.
The MA concluded that:-
• The future course of Mrs E’s health still remained unknown but improvement was
possible.
• The diagnosis remained unclear, with no clear physical cause for her neurological
symptoms.
15

CAS-105605-Z1T5
• A FND was suggested as a cause but this had not yet been confirmed. If following
further assessment FND was diagnosed, then there was still a possibility that her
condition might improve.
• The impact of trauma had not yet been addressed.
• Her ongoing pension and tribunal issues might be impacting on her symptoms.
• It was possible that her joint pain might improve with HRT. If any inflammatory
joint disease was identified, then this could be improved with appropriate
specialist medication.
• The main issue was her joint pain, particularly in the left knee, and involuntary
movement of the left leg. This affected her ability to walk. There was no evidence
to suggest that she has any significant functional impairment of the upper limbs.
• From a physical perspective, Mrs E should be capable of a sedentary desk-based
role. The notes prior to discharge stated that Mrs E was setting up a small
business selling candles online.
• If the medication which she was taking affected her memory and ability to
function, it should be withdrawn.
• “Having reviewed the updated evidence, I remain of the opinion that it does not
support that [Mrs E] will be significantly limited in her ability to achieve gainful
civilian employment until retirement age”.
• There was also the possibility that her condition could improve with further input
and time.
• Ultimately, the MA said that: “A Tier 1 is advised”..
After reviewing all of the available medical evidence at the time, the DO concluded in
its decision letter dated 6 March 2023 that it was satisfied the original decision to
award Mrs E Tier 1 benefit from the AFPS 15 was correct, essentially for the same
reasons given by the MA. Veterans UK subsequently informed Mrs E of the DO’s
decision, with reasons, in its IDRP decision letter dated 7 March 2023.
16

CAS-105605-Z1T5

“As DO, I have reviewed all of the medical evidence including service medical records
including (but not limited to) the final medical board report, the medical opinion of our
own scheme Medical Adviser (MA) and a substantial amount of civilian medical
evidence dealing with both [Mrs E’s] physical conditions as well as her mental health.
Several pieces of medical evidence were obtained and considered as part of the
appeals process, to gain as complete a picture as is possible – of [Mrs E’s] current
level of function, limitations and likely progression of her conditions, whether negative
or positive. In addition to service medical records, consultant neurology letters and
letters from [Mrs E’s] Community Mental Health Nurse have been obtained and
considered. Having considered all of the available evidence, I am satisfied that the
original decision was correct and that Tier 1 benefits are appropriate. In order to
qualify for Tier 2 or Tier 3 awards from the scheme, the scheme manager (delegated
to Veterans UK) must be satisfied that the member is either significantly impaired
from obtaining full-time civilian employment, or has suffered a permanent breakdown
in health involving incapacity for full-time employment, for Tier 2 and Tier 3
respectively. Veterans UK must also be satisfied that incapacity will continue until
normal pension age (60). [Mrs E] is 47 years old.
I concur with medical advisor as well as the specialist opinions in [Mrs E’s] condition.
These opinions confirm that there is the potential for her symptoms to be functional
rather than physical. I understand this to mean that further psychological input would
be required in order to get a full picture of what her condition is and how it can be
treated effectively in the long term.
Her main points of issue in terms of employability appear to be joint pain, particularly
in the left knee involving involuntary movement of the left leg. There is no recent
notes confirming any impairment of the upper limbs. Additionally, [Mrs E’s] memory
has been affected by medication, but it appears from the evidence available that a
plan is in place to reduce medication affecting memory; and that the medication
prescription would most likely be withdrawn by her doctors should her day-to-day
function be significantly impaired.
The medical evidence currently available does not confirm that [Mrs E] is significantly
impaired, and will remain so, until pension age, from achieving any full-time
employment. The medical advisor’s opinion is that she should be capable of a
sedentary role and in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, I accept this
position. I accept that the prognosis for [Mrs E] is unclear and there remains the
potential for both improvement and deterioration. However, until further medical
investigations into the cause for her neurological symptoms are completed, I am
unable to say confidently that [Mrs E] is more likely than not unable to achieve
